content: Pagoda dogwood, scientifically known as Cornus alternifolia and also referred to as alternate-leaved dogwood, is a species of dogwood native to eastern North America. Its range extends from Newfoundland westward to southern Manitoba and Minnesota, and southward to northern Florida and Mississippi. This plant is typically a small deciduous tree, reaching heights of up to 8 meters (occasionally 10 meters) with a trunk diameter of up to 15 centimeters. Its branches grow in distinct horizontal layers, separated by gaps, giving it a characteristic tiered appearance. The leaves of Cornus alternifolia are elliptic to ovate in shape, measuring 4–12 cm in length and 2–6 cm in width. Unlike most other species in the Cornus genus, the leaves are arranged alternately along the stems rather than in opposite pairs. They often cluster densely at the ends of twigs, creating an almost whorled appearance. The upper surface of the leaves is smooth and green, while the underside is hairy and bluish in color. The bark of the tree is gray to brown, becoming ridged as the tree matures. This species produces small, cream-colored flowers with four small petals. These flowers are grouped into inflorescences called cymes, which measure 4–6 cm across. The tree bears fruit resembling berries, which are bluish-black in color and measure 8–10 mm in diameter. Typically, Cornus alternifolia grows as a shrub with multiple stems emerging from the ground, but it can also develop into a small tree with a flat-topped, bushy crown that can reach up to 25 feet in height. It is commonly found along forest margins, beneath open deciduous trees, or near the edges of swamps and forests, thriving in moist, well-drained soils. The tree is considered visually appealing due to its wide-spreading, tiered branches and flat-topped canopy, making it a popular choice for ornamental plantings. The flower clusters of this species lack the large white bracts seen in flowering dogwood (Cornus florida), and its fruit is dark purple with a strong, unpleasant aromatic flavor, unlike the red fruit of Cornus florida. The bark is dark reddish-brown with shallow ridges, while the young branchlets are initially pale reddish-green, later turning dark green. The wood is reddish-brown with pale sapwood, and it is heavy, hard, and fine-grained. Winter buds are light chestnut brown and pointed, with inner scales that enlarge as the shoot grows, eventually reaching half an inch in length before falling off. The leaves are alternate, rarely opposite, and often clustered at the ends of branches. They are simple, measuring 3–5 inches in length and 2–3 inches in width, with an oval or ovate shape. The base of the leaf is wedge-shaped or rounded, and the margins are wavy-toothed and slightly reflexed. The apex is acuminate. When emerging from the bud, the leaves are involute, reddish-green on the upper surface, and coated with silvery-white tomentum on the underside. When fully grown, the leaves are bright green above and pale, downy, and nearly white beneath. They are feather-veined, with a broad, yellowish midrib that is prominent on the underside and about six pairs of primary veins. In autumn, the leaves turn yellow or a combination of yellow and scarlet. The petioles are slender, grooved, hairy, and have clasping bases. The flowers bloom in April and May. They are perfect (having both male and female reproductive structures) and cream-colored, borne in broad, open cymes at the ends of short lateral branches. The calyx is cup-shaped, and the flowers have four valvate petals that open when in bloom. The petals are cream-colored, oblong, and rounded at the ends. Both the petals and stamens are inserted on a disk, with the stamens arranged alternately to the petals. There are four stamens, which are exserted with long, slender filaments. The anthers are oblong, introrse, versatile, and two-celled, with the cells opening longitudinally. The pistil consists of an inferior ovary with two cells, a columnar style, and a capitate stigma. The fruit is a drupe, globular in shape, and blue-black in color, measuring about one-third of an inch across. It is tipped with a remnant of the style, which rises from a slight depression. The nut inside is obovoid and has multiple grooves. The fruit ripens in October.
